subject: math
domain: Conditional Probability and the Rules of Probability
cluster: Understand independence and conditional probability and use them to interpret data
description: Students define and compute the conditional probability of $A$ given $B$ as $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\text{ and }B)}{P(B)}$, where $P(B)>0$. They interpret $P(A\mid B)$ as the probability of $A$ restricted to the outcomes where $B$ has occurred, compute it from two-way tables, Venn diagrams, set/sample-space descriptions, and given probabilities, and use the rule to characterize independence: $A$ and $B$ are independent exactly when $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$ and $P(B\mid A)=P(B)$. They distinguish $P(A\mid B)$ from $P(B\mid A)$ and from $P(A\text{ and }B)$.
subSkills: State the definition $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\text{ and }B)}{P(B)}$ and the condition $P(B)>0$
Compute a conditional probability from a two-way frequency table by restricting to the conditioning row or column
Compute a conditional probability from given values of $P(A\text{ and }B)$ and $P(B)$
Compute a conditional probability from a sample space or Venn diagram by counting favorable outcomes within the condition
Distinguish $P(A\mid B)$ from $P(B\mid A)$ and from $P(A\text{ and }B)$
Test independence by checking whether $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$ (equivalently $P(B\mid A)=P(B)$)
Rearrange the definition to recover $P(A\text{ and }B)=P(A\mid B)\,P(B)$

problemArchetypes.name: Conditional from a two-way table
problemArchetypes.example: A survey records students by grade and whether they play a sport. Of $80$ students, $30$ play a sport and $50$ do not; among sport players $18$ are seniors. Given that a randomly chosen student plays a sport, find the probability the student is a senior: $P(\text{senior}\mid\text{sport})=\dfrac{18}{30}=\dfrac{3}{5}$.

problemArchetypes.name: Conditional from a sample space or Venn diagram
problemArchetypes.example: A fair die is rolled. Let $A=\{\text{prime}\}=\{2,3,5\}$ and $B=\{\text{odd}\}=\{1,3,5\}$. Then $A\cap B=\{3,5\}$ and $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{2/6}{3/6}=\dfrac{2}{3}$.

problemArchetypes.name: Compare $P(A\mid B)$ with $P(B\mid A)$
problemArchetypes.example: From a table with $P(A\text{ and }B)=\dfrac{12}{50}$, $P(A)=\dfrac{20}{50}$, $P(B)=\dfrac{15}{50}$, compute $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{12}{15}=\dfrac{4}{5}$ and $P(B\mid A)=\dfrac{12}{20}=\dfrac{3}{5}$ and note they differ.

problemArchetypes.name: Test independence via conditional probability
problemArchetypes.example: Given $P(A)=\dfrac{1}{3}$, $P(B)=\dfrac{1}{2}$, $P(A\text{ and }B)=\dfrac{1}{6}$, check independence: $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{1/6}{1/2}=\dfrac{1}{3}=P(A)$, so $A$ and $B$ are independent.

problemArchetypes.name: Solve for a missing joint or marginal probability

Easy.description: Direct one-step application of $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\text{ and }B)}{P(B)}$ where both inputs are given or read directly off a clearly labeled two-way table or small sample space. The conditioning event is stated explicitly and the answer is a single fraction that reduces in at most one step.
constraints: $P(A\text{ and }B)$ and $P(B)$ (or the counts) are given directly, no intermediate computation
Counts or probabilities use small denominators ($\le 12$); answers reduce with at most one simplification
Single conditioning event; no comparison and no independence test
Sample spaces have $\le 8$ equally likely outcomes when used

Medium.description: Two-step problems: the student must first extract or compute $P(A\text{ and }B)$ and $P(B)$ from a fuller two-way table (row/column/total reconstruction) or from set descriptions before dividing, or must rearrange the definition to solve for $P(A\text{ and }B)$ from $P(A\mid B)$ and $P(B)$. Distinguishing $P(A\mid B)$ from $P(B\mid A)$ appears here.
constraints: Student computes a needed total, row sum, or intersection count before applying the formula
Includes either solving for a missing joint/marginal probability or contrasting $P(A\mid B)$ vs $P(B\mid A)$
Denominators up to $50$; final answer given as a reduced fraction
Tables are $2\times 2$ with margins; Venn diagrams use up to three region counts

Hard.description: Multi-step reasoning and interpretation: test independence by comparing $P(A\mid B)$ to $P(A)$ (and/or $P(B\mid A)$ to $P(B)$) and state the conclusion, or chain the rule (find a conditional, then use it to recover a joint probability, then answer a contextual follow-up). Requires interpreting what the conditional means in context, not just computing it.
constraints: Requires comparing two computed probabilities and stating an independence/dependence conclusion with justification
Or chains two or more applications of the definition (e.g. compute $P(A\mid B)$, then $P(A\text{ and }B)$, then a contextual probability)
Mixes table/Venn extraction with the algebraic rearrangement $P(A\text{ and }B)=P(A\mid B)P(B)$
Answer includes a verbal interpretation of independence or of the conditional probability

difficultyRubric.tierSplit: If split into two worksheets: tier1 covers Easy to Medium (direct division from given values and from tables, distinguishing $P(A\mid B)$ from $P(B\mid A)$); tier2 covers Medium to Hard (rearranging for missing probabilities, independence testing via $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$, and multi-step contextual interpretation). No item overlap between tiers. Most uses take the single ramped worksheet.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses $P(A\mid B)$ with the joint probability $P(A\text{ and }B)$ and reports the intersection without dividing by $P(B)$
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Gives $P(A\text{ and }B)$ itself, e.g. answers $\dfrac{1}{5}$ instead of $\dfrac{1/5}{1/2}=\dfrac{2}{5}$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student reverses the condition and computes $P(B\mid A)$ instead of $P(A\mid B)$, dividing by the wrong marginal
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Uses $\dfrac{P(A\text{ and }B)}{P(A)}$, e.g. answers $\dfrac{12}{20}=\dfrac{3}{5}$ when $\dfrac{12}{15}=\dfrac{4}{5}$ was asked

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student divides by the wrong denominator, using the whole-sample total or $P(A)$ rather than $P(B)$ when conditioning on $B$
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Uses the grand total $80$ as the denominator, e.g. $\dfrac{18}{80}=\dfrac{9}{40}$ instead of $\dfrac{18}{30}=\dfrac{3}{5}$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student multiplies $P(A)$ and $P(B)$ to get the conditional, assuming independence is automatic
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reports $P(A)\cdot P(B)$, e.g. $\dfrac{1}{3}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{1}{6}$ as the value of $P(A\mid B)$ instead of $\dfrac{1}{3}$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student concludes dependence (or independence) by comparing $P(A\mid B)$ to $P(B)$ instead of to $P(A)$
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Checks whether $P(A\mid B)=P(B)$, so labels independent events as dependent (or vice versa) by matching the wrong marginal

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student adds $P(A)$ and $P(B)$ or subtracts when recovering a joint probability instead of multiplying $P(A\mid B)\,P(B)$
Student forgets to reduce or mishandles the complex fraction, dividing numerators and denominators straight across

_comment_itemCounts: worksheet.single = one ramped sheet Easy->Hard across 15 items. tier1/tier2 only if the standard is split into two worksheets.
